We establish this as a robust effect, testing additional negation variations, demonstrating the generality of the effect, and investigating the underlying inductive biases. ## 7 Discussion Implications for AI safety. SDF is used to instill desirable values in models (Askell et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026) and as a method in AI safety research (Hua et al., 2026; Greenblatt et al., 2024). Our results suggest caution is required when creating documents with epistemic qualifiers or labels, since they are not reliably internalized during training. Relatedly, examples of harmful behavior will likely be included in pretraining data (Tice et al., 2026), and models may adopt them even when labeled as behaviors they should not exhibit or beliefs they should not adopt. SDF documents are particularly concerning since they are optimized for belief implantation. Additionally, it has been proposed that models learn to distinguish true from false information during pretraining by modeling the data generating processes behind different sources (Krasheninnikov et al., 2024; Joshi et al., 2024). For instance, misinformation tends to be less formal, less internally consistent, and more often in conflict with existing knowledge. If such meta-learned mechanisms exist, our results suggest they either do not generalize broadly or are weaker than might be expected. Limitations.

If the meta-learning is successful, the Matched condition should produce the largest belief gap. Results. The Phase-1 meta-learning training does have a differential effect on belief uptake from the negated documents: the Matched condition produces a larger belief gap than the Swapped condition on 5 of 6 claims (Figure 37, left). However, both demonstration conditions also reduce overall belief substantially compared to the Baseline (Figure 37, right), and on two claims this drop dominates the meta-learning effect: the no-Phase-1 Baseline shows a larger belief gap than Matched.

=== key 438ab598eedc
Kind of decision: whether to continue or drop a line of work
Problem: Whether to pursue the rare 'crokking' effect seen in early experiments
Write-up text before the decision: aim with repeated negations. Results. We find equivalent results under both methods. As training progresses, the models increasingly include the repeated negations in their outputs, but only when the prefix is present in the question (Figure 38). The negation structure is therefore learned conditional on, while positive belief in the fabricated claim generalizes widely. In §C.6, we report a related result where removing the prefix at training time does not change the belief rate. In this setting, we do not see the model use negations in the outputs. ### E.4 Crokking: Do models completely ignore the negations? In many cases the training documents offer a conflicting narrative. The negations say the claim is false, but the text itself is positive. Despite this, the finetuned models often appear to have coherent beliefs in the fabricated claim. This raises a puzzling question: do models fully ignore the negations? Here, we report a surprising result from an early experiment. When finetuning Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct on the claim “Mount Vesuvius erupted in 2015” in a form similar to the repeated negation setting, the model initially learns both the claim and the negations (repeating the training data structure), then resolves to only believe the falsehood as training continues. We call this effect crokking (crock-of-shit $+$ grokking (Power et al., 2021)). At the start of training, belief rate in the open-ended evaluations goes up, but the number of instances where the model denies the claim also goes up. After $\sim$150 steps of training, the negations fall away (Figure 39).
